implementation_notes: Java methods are void by convention, so the interesting-return-value discipline appears as deliberate API choices: Map.put returns the value it replaced, Set.add returns whether the collection changed, Optional<T> (Java 8) replaces a bare null when there is nothing to return, and Stream operators return new values instead of mutating in place. Because javac does not warn about ignored results, enforcement comes from static analysis annotations such as CheckReturnValue (Error Prone), so the convention has to be established method by method. The plain void setter is still right when nothing interesting happened, and Optional on every getter is overkill.
code_sketch:
Optional<User> found = users.find(id);
if (found.isPresent()) { render(found.get()); }  // no null, no 2nd lookup

User previous = cache.put(id, user);   // the replaced value is the result
boolean changed = tags.add("urgent");  // did anything change?
pitfalls: Nothing in javac warns about a discarded result: cache.put(k, v) for the previous value, or an unwrapped Optional, compiles silently unless an annotation processor or linter is configured.
Optional is not for fields, parameters or every getter - it allocates and pushes the unwrapping onto callers; use it where absence is a normal outcome of the method's work.

A map-like API that returns the previous value can only be read that way if it documents it, and implementations that allow null values cannot distinguish 'no previous value' from 'previous value was null'.

variants.name: Fluent self-returning builder
variants.implementation_notes: The receiver-returning realization in Java: every configuration step returns this - StringBuilder.append has done so since Java 1.5, and generated builders such as Lombok's @Builder follow the same shape - so a construction reads as one chained expression ending in build(). Use it for configuration and collection APIs where the caller's next act is another call on the same object; avoid it on a domain type's setters, where it hides mutation and leaks the concrete class out of the interface.
pitfalls: A fluent chain returns the concrete type, so it breaks when a factory hands back an interface or a dynamic proxy.
Chained mutators read like queries: a statement such as account.deposit(10).close() hides two state changes in one expression.
